paras: The lynching of Hickman was the killing of a man named Hickman by a mob of about seventy-five men at Boston, Colorado, in early October 1888. Hickman was accused of having shot and killed J. C. Booth, a man who had been visiting the woman Hickman lived with, and the mob took him from his house within hours and hanged him. The story reached the national press as a brief Trinidad dispatch and was reprinted in papers from Georgia to Dakota over the following two weeks.

According to a Trinidad special in the Fort Worth Gazette, Hickman had for some time had a woman living with him who was "ostensibly proving up a claim" but was "generally known as Hickman's mistress." Booth had lately been paying her attention, and rumor had it that the two were to be married. The wire version said only that Booth was "in the habit of paying visits" to the woman.

The Gazette's account said that when Booth visited the woman, Hickman ran him off the place and fired a shotgun at him without effect. Hickman then went back to the house, reloaded, overtook Booth and killed him with a load of shot in the breast before returning home. Once the killing became known, a mob of about seventy-five men went to Hickman's house, took him out and "strung him up to a convenient limb." The wire version put the lynching an hour after the shooting, while the Gazette said "a few hours later."
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named a member of the mob.

Most papers carried a four-line dispatch, credited by the Savannah Morning News to the Denver Republican's special from Trinidad, under headlines such as "Lynched in Colorado," "Lynched by a Mob" and "A Colorado Lynching." That text called Hickman "the murderer" and gave no comment on the mob. A Denver rewrite dated October 6 ran as "A Life for a Life" and "A Murder and a Lynching," reducing the cause to "a quarrel about a woman."

The Fort Worth Gazette printed the only fuller account, headed "A Convenient Liab" [Limb], which described the killing of Booth as "cold-blooded" and "cowardly" and the lynchers as "indignant citizens" whose indignation "knew no bounds." Telegraphic-brief columns in Indianapolis and Wheeling and weekly digests in the Northwest condensed the story to a sentence, the Bismarck Weekly Tribune noting only that "A murderer named Hickman was lynched at Boston, Col." The item was still running in Minnesota and Dakota weeklies on October 17 and 18. None of the accounts mentions the race of Hickman or Booth.

Accounts differ on the date: the Wheeling Intelligencer said the lynching happened "last night" and weekly digests put the shooting "on the 5th," while the Fort Worth special said the murder was "perpetrated near there on the 2nd inst." The October 5 dates may reflect the dispatch dateline, though the Fort Worth report was itself secondhand news brought to Trinidad by visitors from Boston. The Wheeling item also placed the lynching at Trinidad rather than Boston, and some digests printed Booth's initials as "J. P."

reader.title: Lynching of Hickman
bases: Every account says a mob of about seventy-five men took Hickman from his home and lynched him after he was said to have shot Booth (A3, A6, A2).

A mob of about seventy-five men took Hickman from his house and hanged him, with no lawful authority mentioned (A3, A6); the Fort Worth account frames it as punishment by 'indignant citizens' for a 'cold-blooded murder' (A5, A6).

Two Trinidad specials, the Denver Republican's wire (A3) and a separately written Fort Worth Gazette dispatch with different details (A5, A6), agree on the killing of Booth and the lynching of Hickman by about seventy-five men, though both rest on reports brought to Trinidad from Boston.

accounts.gist: Visitors from Boston reported a murder on the 2nd: Hickman ran Booth off, fired a shotgun that missed, reloaded, overtook and killed him; a few hours later about seventy-five men hanged Hickman from a limb.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the four-line Trinidad wire under headlines such as 'Lynched in Colorado', 'Lynched by a Mob' and 'A Colorado Lynching', calling Hickman 'the murderer' without comment.
The Fort Worth Gazette called the shooting 'cold-blooded' and 'cowardly' and said 'the indignation of the citizens knew no bounds' before the mob acted.
A Denver Oct. 6 rewrite headed 'A Life for a Life' reduced the cause to 'a quarrel about a woman'.
